# Brake Caliper Assembly

## General Structure

The brake caliper (100) is configured as a two-piece housing, comprising a first part (104a) and a second part (104b) that are joined together to straddle a brake disc. These two parts cooperate to hold a pair of braking members (102a, 102b)—typically brake pads or friction elements—positioned on opposite sides of the disc. The first braking member (102a) is retained within or adjacent to the first part (104a) of the caliper, while the second braking member (102b) is similarly associated with the second part (104b). This dual-part construction allows the caliper to house both a service brake mechanism and a park brake mechanism within a compact, integrated assembly.

## Service Brake Mechanism

To generate the clamping force required for normal braking operations, the service brake mechanism employs at least two piston and cylinder assemblies, identified as (108a, 110a) and (108b, 110b). These assemblies are arranged in an opposed piston configuration, meaning that one piston-cylinder pair is located within the first part of the caliper (104a) and acts upon the first braking member (102a), while the corresponding piston-cylinder pair is located within the second part (104b) and acts upon the second braking member (102b).

During service braking, hydraulic or pneumatic pressure is delivered simultaneously to both cylinders (110a, 110b), causing the pistons (108a, 108b) to extend outward from their respective cylinders. This coordinated, opposed actuation pushes each braking member independently and symmetrically toward the brake disc from both sides, ensuring balanced clamping force distribution and even pad wear. Because the pistons act directly on their respective braking members without relying on a mechanical linkage between the two caliper halves, the service brake mechanism operates independently of the park brake components described below.

## Park Brake Mechanism

In addition to the service brake mechanism, the caliper (100) integrates a park brake mechanism designed to hold the vehicle stationary without requiring continuous hydraulic pressure. This mechanism includes an actuator mechanism (112), which may take the form of an electric motor, a mechanical cam, a spring-loaded device, or another suitable actuation means. The actuator mechanism (112) is configured to generate and apply a driving force directly to the first braking member (102a), pushing it toward the brake disc in a manner similar to the action produced by the service brake piston.

However, unlike the service brake mechanism—which independently actuates both braking members through separate opposed pistons—the park brake mechanism applies force to only one side of the caliper directly. To achieve clamping on both sides of the disc, the driving force generated at the first braking member (102a) must be transferred across the caliper to the second braking member (102b).

## Force Transmitting Member

To accomplish this transfer of force, the caliper incorporates a force transmitting member (116). This component is responsible for conveying the park brake actuator's driving force from the first braking member (102a), where the force originates, to the second opposed braking member (102b) on the other side of the disc. In effect, as the actuator mechanism (112) pushes the first braking member toward the brake disc, the force transmitting member (116) reacts against this movement and transmits a corresponding force to the second braking member, drawing or pushing it into contact with the opposite face of the disc. This arrangement enables a single actuator to produce a balanced, two-sided clamping force despite being mechanically coupled to only one braking member directly.

## Support and Mounting of the Force Transmitting Member

To function reliably under the loads generated during park brake application, the force transmitting member (116) is supported at two locations along its length. First, it maintains a sliding connection with the outer surface of the first cylinder (110a), which is part of the service brake piston-cylinder assembly located in the first caliper part (104a). This sliding interface allows the force transmitting member to move axially relative to the first cylinder while remaining radially supported and guided by it, ensuring proper alignment during actuation.

Second, the force transmitting member (116) engages in a slidable connection with a connecting member that spans across both parts of the caliper, bridging the first part (104a) and the second part (104b). This connecting member provides a structural link between the two caliper halves, and its slidable interface with the force transmitting member permits relative axial movement while maintaining consistent positioning and load transfer capability.

Together, these two support points—the sliding connection with the first cylinder's outer surface and the slidable engagement with the cross-caliper connecting member—allow the force transmitting member to translate axially in response to actuator-induced movement of the first braking member, while remaining properly guided and constrained within the overall caliper structure. This dual-support arrangement ensures that the force transmitting member can reliably and consistently deliver the park brake's clamping force to the second braking member, enabling effective and balanced parking brake engagement across both sides of the brake disc.

# Brake Caliper Assembly with Integrated Service and Park Brake Mechanisms

## Background

Brake calipers used in vehicle braking systems must reliably perform two distinct functions: providing service braking force during normal driving operations and maintaining a secure parking brake engagement when the vehicle is stationary. Achieving both functions within a single, compact caliper assembly while ensuring consistent force distribution across the braking members presents ongoing design challenges, particularly with respect to the stability and durability of the force transmission components.

## Detailed Description

The brake caliper (100) disclosed herein comprises a first part (104a) and a second part (104b), which together define a housing structure configured to hold and position a pair of braking members (102a, 102b) on opposite sides of a brake disc. The first part (104a) and second part (104b) are connected to one another, typically by a bridge or connecting structure, so as to straddle the disc and maintain proper alignment of the braking members relative to the friction surfaces of the disc.

### Service Brake Mechanism

To provide normal, everyday braking functionality, the caliper (100) incorporates a service brake mechanism built around opposed piston and cylinder assemblies. Specifically, a first piston and cylinder assembly (108a, 110a) is housed within the first part (104a), and a second piston and cylinder assembly (108b, 110b) is housed within the second part (104b). These two assemblies are arranged in an opposed configuration, meaning that when hydraulic or pneumatic pressure is applied to the pistons (108a, 108b) within their respective cylinders (110a, 110b), the pistons extend outward from opposite sides of the disc simultaneously. This opposed actuation causes the braking members (102a, 102b) to be pressed against the corresponding friction surfaces of the disc from both sides, generating the clamping force necessary for service braking. The design ensures balanced force application across the disc, minimizing uneven wear on the braking members and providing consistent, predictable braking performance during routine vehicle operation.

### Park Brake Mechanism

In addition to the service brake mechanism, the caliper (100) is equipped with a park brake mechanism designed to maintain braking engagement without requiring continuous application of hydraulic or pneumatic pressure. This mechanism includes an actuator (112), which may be electrically, mechanically, or otherwise powered, and which is configured to generate the force required to engage the parking brake function. The actuator (112) works in conjunction with a force transmitting member (116), which serves as the critical link between the actuator and the braking members (102a, 102b).

The force transmitting member (116) is responsible for converting the output of the actuator (112) into a mechanical force capable of driving both braking members (102a, 102b) into engagement with the disc, thereby securing the vehicle in a stationary position. Because the force transmitting member must span across the caliper and interact with components on both the first part (104a) and second part (104b), its structural support and alignment are of particular importance to ensure reliable operation over the life of the caliper.

### Dual Sliding Support of the Force Transmitting Member

A key feature of this design is the manner in which the force transmitting member (116) achieves stable, well-supported movement as it transmits parking brake force. Rather than relying on a single point or type of support, the force transmitting member (116) is supported through two distinct sliding connections, each contributing to overall stability and precise alignment during actuation.

The first sliding connection is established between the force transmitting member (116) and the outer surface of the first cylinder (110a). This connection allows the force transmitting member to slide smoothly along the exterior of the cylinder, using the cylinder itself as a guide surface. This arrangement takes advantage of the existing structural rigidity and fixed positioning of the first cylinder (110a) within the first part (104a) of the caliper, providing a stable reference surface without the need for additional dedicated guide components.

The second sliding connection is formed between the force transmitting member (116) and a connecting member that spans both the first part (104a) and second part (104b) of the caliper. This connecting member, which bridges the two sides of the caliper housing, provides an additional support point that helps maintain the orientation and alignment of the force transmitting member as it moves to engage the braking members. By sliding along this connecting member, the force transmitting member is prevented from tilting, twisting, or otherwise deviating from its intended path of motion during actuation.

Together, these two sliding connections—one referencing the first cylinder (110a) and the other referencing the connecting member spanning both caliper parts—provide the force transmitting member (116) with dual-point support. This dual support arrangement significantly enhances the stability of the force transmitting member during operation, ensuring that the force generated by the actuator (112) is transmitted efficiently and evenly to both braking members (102a, 102b).

### Advantages of the Design

The combination of these two sliding connections offers several advantages over single-point support arrangements. First, the dual support reduces the likelihood of misalignment or binding of the force transmitting member (116) during park brake engagement, which might otherwise result in uneven force distribution between the braking members (102a, 102b). Second, by utilizing the outer surface of the existing first cylinder (110a) as one of the sliding surfaces, the design minimizes the need for additional dedicated structural components, thereby reducing manufacturing complexity and cost. Third, the use of a connecting member that spans both parts of the caliper as the second sliding support ensures that the force transmitting member remains properly guided relative to both the first part (104a) and second part (104b), even as the components experience the mechanical stresses associated with repeated park brake actuation.

As a result of this dual sliding support configuration, the force transmitting member (116) is able to reliably and efficiently transmit the parking brake force generated by the actuator (112) to both braking members (102a, 102b), ensuring consistent, balanced engagement of the parking brake across the disc. This design contributes to improved durability, reduced wear, and enhanced overall reliability of the park brake mechanism, while maintaining compatibility with the opposed piston and cylinder assemblies (108a, 110a and 108b, 110b) used for service braking within the same integrated caliper assembly (100).

# The Definite Article: A Small Word with Big Significance

"The" is one of the most frequently used words in the English language, serving as the definite article. Despite its brevity—just three letters—it plays a crucial grammatical role in everyday communication.

## Function and Purpose

The primary function of "the" is to specify a particular noun that both the speaker and listener understand or have previously discussed. Unlike the indefinite articles "a" and "an," which introduce something general or unspecified, "the" points to something specific. For example:

- "I saw a dog" (any dog, unspecified)
- "I saw the dog" (a particular dog, known to both parties)

## Historical Origins

The word "the" evolved from Old English, where it developed from demonstrative pronouns like "se," "seo," and "þæt," which meant "that" or "this." Over centuries, these forms simplified into the single, gender-neutral word we use today. This evolution reflects the broader simplification of English grammar, which once had more complex inflections similar to German or Latin.

## Frequency and Importance

Linguistic studies consistently show that "the" is the most common word in written and spoken English, appearing far more often than any other word. Its ubiquity makes it essential for:

- **Clarity**: Distinguishing specific items from general categories
- **Cohesion**: Linking ideas across sentences by referring back to previously mentioned nouns
- **Natural flow**: Providing rhythm and structure to sentences

## Challenges for Learners

For non-native English speakers, mastering the use of "the" can be surprisingly difficult. Many languages either lack articles entirely (like Russian or Japanese) or use them differently. Learners often struggle with:

- When to omit "the" entirely (e.g., "I like music" vs. "I like the music of Bach")
- Using "the" with proper nouns (e.g., "the Netherlands" vs. simply "France")
- Applying "the" in idiomatic expressions that don't follow standard rules

## Conclusion

Though easily overlooked due to its simplicity, "the" is foundational to English syntax and meaning. Its proper use requires an intuitive grasp of context, specificity, and convention—making it a small word that carries significant linguistic weight.

# Patent Abstract

**OPPOSED-PISTON BRAKE CALIPER WITH INTEGRATED PARK BRAKE ACTUATOR**

An opposed-piston brake caliper assembly integrates a hydraulic service brake mechanism with a mechanically or electromechanically actuated parking brake system within a unified caliper housing. The caliper comprises a rigid body defining opposed cylinder bores positioned on either side of a brake disc, each housing a piston configured to translate axially and apply clamping force to friction pads engaging the disc from opposite faces, thereby providing balanced, symmetric loading during service braking operations.

At least one piston within the opposed-piston arrangement is configured as a dual-function piston, incorporating an integrated ball-and-ramp mechanism, screw-and-nut assembly, or equivalent force-conversion device coupled to a park brake actuator. The actuator, which may be electrically driven via a motor-gear reduction unit or mechanically actuated via a cable linkage, converts rotational input into axial thrust, displacing the dual-function piston to maintain clamping force independent of hydraulic pressure. A self-locking mechanism, such as a irreversible screw thread or mechanical detent, retains the piston in the clamped position without continuous power or hydraulic pressure input, enabling sustained parking brake engagement.

The integrated design allows the park brake actuator to utilize the same piston and pad interface as the service brake, eliminating the need for a separate parking brake caliper, drum-in-hat mechanism, or auxiliary actuator assembly. Seals and guide arrangements isolate the hydraulic circuit from the mechanical actuator components, preventing fluid ingress into the actuator while permitting relative motion between the piston and housing. This configuration reduces overall system mass, package volume, and component count while enabling automatic or manual park brake release through reversal of the actuator, and supports compatibility with electronic parking brake control systems for dynamic engagement during vehicle operation.

# PATENT DISCLOSURE

## TITLE OF INVENTION
**BRAKE CALIPER ASSEMBLY WITH DUAL PISTON-CYLINDER ARRANGEMENT AND UNIFIED PARKING BRAKE FORCE TRANSMISSION MEMBER**

---

## FIELD OF THE INVENTION

The present disclosure relates generally to vehicle braking systems, and more particularly to a brake caliper assembly incorporating two independent piston-cylinder assemblies for service braking, in combination with a single force transmitting member that mechanically couples a parking brake actuator to both an inboard and an outboard brake pad, thereby enabling simultaneous parking brake application at both friction interfaces through a unified actuation mechanism.

---

## BACKGROUND OF THE INVENTION

Conventional disc brake calipers used in automotive and heavy-vehicle applications typically employ hydraulic piston-cylinder assemblies to apply clamping force to brake pads positioned on either side of a brake rotor during normal service braking operations. Many such calipers additionally incorporate a mechanically actuated parking brake mechanism to provide static vehicle restraint independent of the hydraulic system, which may lose pressure over time or in the event of system failure.

In many existing designs, the parking brake mechanism acts upon only one piston or one pad directly, relying upon caliper housing deflection, floating caliper movement, or hydraulic fluid displacement between chambers to transmit clamping force to the opposing pad. Such arrangements can suffer from several disadvantages, including:

1. Uneven or delayed force application between the inboard and outboard brake pads during parking brake engagement;
2. Increased reliance on caliper frame rigidity and bushing/slide-pin tolerances to achieve balanced clamping, which may degrade with wear, corrosion, or contamination;
3. Reduced parking brake holding force efficiency due to lost motion or compliance in the force transfer path;
4. Increased complexity and part count when separate actuators or linkages are required for each pad.

There exists a need for a brake caliper design that provides direct, balanced, and efficient mechanical force transmission from a single parking brake actuator to both brake pads, while retaining independent hydraulic piston-cylinder assemblies for normal service braking.

---

## SUMMARY OF THE INVENTION

The present disclosure provides a brake caliper assembly comprising:

(a) a caliper housing defining a first cylinder bore and a second cylinder bore, each bore slidably receiving a respective piston;

(b) a first piston-cylinder assembly disposed to act upon an inboard brake pad, and a second piston-cylinder assembly disposed to act upon an outboard brake pad, each piston-cylinder assembly being in fluid communication with a hydraulic service brake circuit;

(c) a parking brake actuator mounted to or supported by the caliper housing, operable to generate a mechanical actuation force independent of hydraulic pressure; and

(d) a force transmitting member operatively coupled to the parking brake actuator and extending therefrom into mechanical engagement with both the inboard brake pad (directly or through the first piston) and the outboard brake pad (directly or through the second piston), such that actuation of the parking brake actuator causes the force transmitting member to simultaneously apply clamping force to both brake pads independent of hydraulic pressure in either piston-cylinder assembly.

In this manner, a single parking brake actuator and a single force transmitting member achieve balanced, direct mechanical clamping of both brake pads, eliminating the need for the caliper housing itself to serve as the primary reactive load path during parking brake engagement, and improving consistency of parking brake holding force.

---

## DETAILED DESCRIPTION OF THE INVENTION

### 1. General Caliper Structure

Referring to the disclosed embodiment, the brake caliper assembly (10) comprises a caliper housing (12) straddling a brake rotor (14), the rotor (14) having a first friction surface (14a) and an opposing second friction surface (14b). The caliper housing (12) defines a first cylinder bore (16) and a second cylinder bore (18), positioned on opposite sides of the rotor (14).

A first piston (20) is slidably received within the first cylinder bore (16), and a second piston (22) is slidably received within the second cylinder bore (18). The first piston (20) bears against, or is coupled to, an inboard brake pad (24), while the second piston (22) bears against, or is coupled to, an outboard brake pad (26). Each of the inboard brake pad (24) and outboard brake pad (26) is positioned to frictionally engage a respective friction surface (14a, 14b) of the rotor (14).

The first cylinder bore (16) and second cylinder bore (18) are each in fluid communication with a hydraulic service brake circuit (28), such that pressurized hydraulic fluid delivered to the bores (16, 18) urges the pistons (20, 22) axially outward against their respective brake pads (24, 26), thereby generating clamping force for normal service braking.

### 2. Parking Brake Actuator

The caliper assembly (10) further comprises a parking brake actuator (30) mounted to the caliper housing (12), positioned at or near the second cylinder bore (18) in one embodiment, though alternative mounting locations are contemplated. The parking brake actuator (30) may comprise, without limitation:

- An electric motor-driven spindle or ball-ramp mechanism;
- A cable-actuated lever and screw mechanism;
- A pneumatic or vacuum-actuated diaphragm coupled to a mechanical output shaft; or
- Any equivalent mechanical, electromechanical, or electro-hydraulic actuator capable of generating a linear or rotary output force independent of hydraulic brake pressure.

The parking brake actuator (30) produces an actuation output, illustratively an axial thrust or rotary torque converted to axial thrust via an internal ball-and-ramp or screw mechanism, which is transmitted to a force transmitting member as described below.

### 3. Force Transmitting Member

A key inventive feature of the present disclosure is a force transmitting member (32) operatively interposed between the parking brake actuator (30) and both the inboard brake pad (24) and outboard brake pad (26).

In one embodiment, the force transmitting member (32) comprises an elongated rigid or semi-rigid element extending axially through, alongside, or externally to the caliper housing (12), having:

- A **first end (32a)** operatively coupled to the parking brake actuator (30), such that actuation of the actuator (30) imparts an axial or rotational displacement to the force transmitting member (32);
- A **second end (32b)** engaging the second piston (22) or the outboard brake pad (26) directly, such that displacement of the force transmitting member (32) urges the outboard brake pad (26) into contact with the rotor friction surface (14b); and
- An **intermediate portion (32c)** or a coupling extension operatively linked to the first piston (20) or inboard brake pad (24), such that reactive or transmitted force is simultaneously conveyed to urge the inboard brake pad (24) into contact with the rotor friction surface (14a).

In an alternative embodiment, the force transmitting member (32) comprises a bridging strut, yoke, or crossbar extending across the caliper housing (12), rigidly or pivotally connected at opposing ends to structural extensions of the first piston (20) and second piston (22), respectively, wherein the parking brake actuator (30) applies its actuation force to a central or intermediate point of the bridging member, causing simultaneous and substantially equal displacement of both pistons (20, 22), and consequently both brake pads (24, 26), toward the rotor (14).

In yet another embodiment, the force transmitting member (32) comprises a push-rod and reaction-rod pair mechanically linked through the parking brake actuator (30) housing itself, such that the actuator housing serves as a reactive abutment, and actuation causes the push-rod to advance the second piston (22)/outboard pad (26) while the reaction-rod, through a lever or cam arrangement, simultaneously draws or advances the first piston (20)/inboard pad (24).

### 4. Mode of Operation

**Service Braking:** During normal service braking, hydraulic fluid pressure is independently delivered to the first cylinder bore (16) and second cylinder bore (18), causing the first piston (20) and second piston (22) to independently advance and apply clamping force to the inboard brake pad (24) and outboard brake pad (26), respectively. The force transmitting member (32) remains substantially passive during this mode, save for its structural coupling role, and does not resist or interfere with independent hydraulic piston movement, owing to permissible lost-motion, slip-joint, or compliant coupling features described in various embodiments.

**Parking Brake Application:** Upon actuation of the parking brake actuator (30), the actuator generates an axial or rotary output force that is transmitted through the force transmitting member (32) to both the inboard brake pad (24) and outboard brake pad (26) simultaneously, via the mechanical linkages described above. This mechanical force is independent of hydraulic pressure and remains effective even in the absence of hydraulic fluid pressure, providing a static holding force sufficient to prevent vehicle movement.

**Release:** Deactivation or reversal of the parking brake actuator (30) permits the force transmitting member (32) to retract, releasing mechanical clamping force from both brake pads (24, 26), while the pistons (20, 22) return to their retracted hydraulic rest positions under the influence of piston seal rollback or return springs.

### 5. Advantages

The disclosed arrangement provides several technical advantages over prior art caliper designs:

1. **Balanced Force Distribution:** Because the force transmitting member (32) mechanically couples both brake pads (24, 26) to a single actuator (30), clamping force is applied in a balanced and simultaneous manner, reducing dependence on caliper housing rigidity for force equalization.

2. **Reduced Lost Motion:** Direct mechanical coupling minimizes compliance and lost motion inherent in designs relying on hydraulic fluid displacement or caliper housing flexure to transmit parking brake force to the opposing pad.

3. **Simplified Actuator Requirements:** A single parking brake actuator (30) suffices to actuate both brake pads (24, 26), reducing part count, cost, and packaging complexity compared to dual-actuator designs.

4. **Fail-Safe Operation:** The mechanical force transmission path operates independently of hydraulic pressure, ensuring reliable parking brake function even in the event of hydraulic system failure or fluid loss.

5. **Compatibility:** The disclosed force transmitting member (32) may be retrofitted or adapted to various caliper housing architectures, including fixed and floating caliper designs, without requiring substantial redesign of the hydraulic service brake circuit.

---

# Patent Specification Draft: Floating Caliper Park Brake Assembly

## FIELD OF THE INVENTION

This disclosure relates to vehicle brake systems, and more particularly to a floating caliper disc brake assembly having an integrated parking brake mechanism that actuates a first brake pad and transmits corresponding clamping force to an opposing second brake pad through a slidably engaged connector.

## BACKGROUND

Floating caliper disc brake assemblies typically employ a caliper body slidably mounted on a bracket fixed to a vehicle knuckle or axle, straddling a brake rotor. During service braking, hydraulic pressure acts directly upon a piston to displace an inboard pad into contact with the rotor, while reactive force causes the caliper body to slide and draw an outboard pad into simultaneous contact via a caliper finger or bridge portion.

Integration of a mechanical parking brake function into such floating calipers presents design challenges, particularly with respect to efficiently transmitting actuation force to the pad opposite the parking brake mechanism without introducing excessive lash, misalignment, or binding during the sliding/floating motion inherent to the caliper's operation.

## SUMMARY OF THE INVENTION

According to one aspect of the present disclosure, a floating brake caliper assembly is provided comprising:

a caliper body defining a bore and configured to straddle a brake rotor, the caliper body being slidably supported relative to a mounting bracket along an axis substantially parallel to an axis of rotation of the rotor;

a first brake pad and a second brake pad disposed on opposite sides of the rotor, the caliper body being operable to urge the first and second brake pads into frictional engagement with opposing braking surfaces of the rotor;

a parking brake actuator mechanism operatively coupled to the caliper body and configured to apply an axial actuation force directly to the first brake pad independent of hydraulic pressure within the bore; and

a force-transmitting connector slidably engaged between the parking brake actuator mechanism, or a component driven thereby, and the second brake pad, the connector being configured to transmit the axial actuation force from the first brake pad side of the caliper to the second brake pad such that both the first and second brake pads are urged into clamping engagement with the rotor upon actuation of the parking brake mechanism.

## DETAILED DESCRIPTION

### General Arrangement

Referring to the figures, wherein like reference numerals designate corresponding parts throughout several views, a floating caliper assembly **10** is shown mounted relative to a brake rotor **12** having a first friction surface **14** and an opposing second friction surface **16**. The caliper assembly **10** includes a caliper housing **20** slidably supported on a bracket **22** via one or more guide pins **24**, permitting the caliper housing **20** to translate along an axis **A-A** substantially parallel to the rotational axis of the rotor **12**.

A first brake pad **30** is disposed adjacent the first friction surface **14**, and a second brake pad **32** is disposed adjacent the second friction surface **16**, each pad **30, 32** being carried by the caliper housing **20** or bracket **22** for axial movement toward and away from the rotor **12**.

### Parking Brake Actuator Mechanism

A parking brake actuator mechanism **40** is disposed within or adjacent the caliper housing **20** on a side proximate the first brake pad **30**. In the illustrated embodiment, the parking brake actuator mechanism **40** comprises a rotatable actuator shaft **42** operatively coupled to a mechanical linkage **44**, such as a cable-actuated lever, ball-and-ramp mechanism, or screw-type actuator, configured to convert an input rotational or linear force—received, for example, from a park brake cable **46** or electric motor **48**—into an axial thrust force.

The parking brake actuator mechanism **40** is arranged to bear directly against a back plate **50** of the first brake pad **30**, such that actuation of the mechanism **40** displaces the first brake pad **30** axially into engagement with the first friction surface **14** of the rotor **12**, independent of any hydraulic pressure that may be present within a hydraulic piston bore **60** of the caliper housing **20**.

### Force-Transmitting Connector

To effect corresponding clamping engagement of the second brake pad **32** against the second friction surface **16** of the rotor **12**, a force-transmitting connector **70** is provided. The connector **70** extends across the caliper housing **20**, from a first end **72** operatively associated with the parking brake actuator mechanism **40** or the first brake pad **30**, to a second end **74** engaging the second brake pad **32** or a carrier associated therewith.

In an exemplary embodiment, the connector **70** comprises an elongated member, such as a rod, strap, or bridge element, received within a complementary slot, bore, or channel **76** formed in the caliper housing **20**, such that the connector **70** is permitted to slide axially relative to the caliper housing **20** along an axis substantially parallel to axis **A-A**. This sliding engagement accommodates relative movement between the connector **70** and the caliper housing **20** as the caliper housing **20** floats during both service braking and parking brake actuation, thereby preventing binding and ensuring substantially equal force distribution between the first brake pad **30** and second brake pad **32**.

In one configuration, the first end **72** of the connector **70** is fixed to or abuts a reaction plate **80** positioned behind the first brake pad **30**, such that axial force applied by the parking brake actuator mechanism **40** is reacted through the reaction plate **80** into the connector **70**. The connector **70** transmits this force across the caliper housing **20**—for example, by extending through an internal passage formed longitudinally through a bridge portion **90** of the caliper housing **20** connecting the inboard and outboard legs thereof—to the second end **74**, which bears against the second brake pad **32**, urging it into engagement with the second friction surface **16**.

The sliding interface between the connector **70** and the caliper housing **20** at channel **76** may include a low-friction bushing, sleeve, or coating **78** to facilitate smooth axial translation and to reduce wear resulting from repeated actuation cycles and floating motion of the caliper housing **20** relative to the bracket **22**.

### Operation

During a parking brake application, an operator or automated control system actuates the parking brake actuator mechanism **40**, for instance by pulling cable **46** or energizing motor **48**. This actuation causes linkage **44** to convert input force into axial displacement of the actuator shaft **42**, which bears against the first brake pad **30**, urging it into frictional engagement with the first friction surface **14** of the rotor **12**.

Simultaneously, reactive axial force is transmitted through reaction plate **80** into the first end **72** of connector **70**. Because the connector **70** is slidably received within channel **76**, it is free to move axially relative to the caliper housing **20** while still transmitting the applied force to its second end **74**, which acts upon the second brake pad **32**. This causes the second brake pad **32** to be drawn or pushed into frictional engagement with the second friction surface **16** of the rotor **12**, substantially simultaneously with engagement of the first brake pad **30**, thereby generating a clamping force across the rotor **12** sufficient to hold the vehicle stationary.

Upon release of the parking brake actuator mechanism **40**, the axial force is removed, and the first and second brake pads **30, 32** are permitted to retract from the friction surfaces **14, 16** of the rotor **12**, for example under the bias of one or more return springs (not shown) or through elastic deformation of one or more seals associated with the hydraulic piston.

## ALTERNATIVE EMBODIMENTS

It will be appreciated that the force-transmitting connector **70** may take various alternative forms without departing from the scope of the present disclosure, including but not limited to:

(a) a pair of parallel rods slidably received within corresponding bores formed in the caliper housing **20**;

(b) a U-shaped or C-shaped bridge member slidably engaging an external surface of the caliper housing **20**;

(c) a cable or flexible tension member routed through a guide channel formed in the caliper housing **20**, configured to transmit tensile rather than compressive force to the second brake pad **32**; or

(d) a lever-type connector pivotally mounted to the caliper housing **20** at an intermediate point, with the sliding connector engaging a cam or roller surface to convert the force transmission path.

It will further be appreciated that the parking brake actuator mechanism **40** may be positioned adjacent either the inboard or outboard brake pad, with the force-transmitting connector **70** configured accordingly to transmit force to the opposite pad, without departing from the scope of the claims appended hereto.

## EXEMPLARY CLAIMS

**1.** A floating brake caliper assembly comprising:
a caliper housing slidably mounted relative to a bracket for movement along an axis substantially parallel to a rotational axis of a brake rotor;
a first brake pad and a second brake pad positioned on opposite sides of the brake rotor;
a parking brake actuator mechanism supported by the caliper housing and configured to apply an axial force directly to the first brake pad; and
a connector slidably engaged with the caliper housing and extending between the first brake pad and the second brake pad, the connector being configured to transmit the axial force applied by the parking brake actuator mechanism to the second brake pad, such that actuation of the parking brake actuator mechanism urges both the first brake pad and the second brake pad into frictional engagement with the brake rotor.

**2.** The floating brake caliper assembly of claim 1, wherein the connector is slidably received within a channel formed in a bridge portion of the caliper housing.

**3.** The floating brake caliper assembly of claim 1, wherein the parking brake actuator mechanism comprises a cable-actuated lever mechanism configured to convert rotational input force into axial thrust force.

**4.** The floating brake caliper assembly of claim 1, wherein the parking brake actuator mechanism comprises an electric motor-driven ball-and-ramp mechanism.

**5.** The floating brake caliper assembly of claim 1, further comprising a reaction plate disposed between the parking brake actuator mechanism and the first brake pad, the connector being operatively coupled to the reaction plate.

**6.** The floating brake caliper assembly of claim 1, wherein the connector comprises a low-friction bushing disposed at an interface between the connector and the caliper housing.

**7.** The floating brake caliper assembly of claim 1, wherein the caliper housing further defines a hydraulic piston bore configured to actuate the first brake pad independently of the parking brake actuator mechanism during service braking.

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate an abstract in the style of a mechanical engineering patent for a dual-function brake caliper (service + parking brake) using an opposed piston arrangement and a slidable force transmission member.
counterfactuals.output:
# ABSTRACT

A dual-function brake caliper assembly is disclosed, providing both hydraulic service braking and mechanical parking brake actuation within a unified opposed-piston housing structure. The caliper body defines a pair of opposed cylinder bores positioned on either side of a rotor, each slidably receiving a piston configured for axial displacement toward friction pad assemblies mounted adjacent the rotor's braking surfaces.

At least one of the opposed pistons incorporates a hollow bore configured to receive a slidable force transmission member disposed coaxially therein. This force transmission member is operatively coupled to a mechanical actuation mechanism, comprising a rotatable actuator shaft engaging a thrust component, such that rotational input is converted into axial thrust independent of hydraulic pressure. During service braking, pressurized hydraulic fluid introduced into the opposed cylinder bores displaces both pistons symmetrically toward the rotor, effecting frictional engagement of the pad assemblies against opposing rotor faces.

For parking brake engagement, actuation of the mechanical mechanism drives the force transmission member axially within the hollow piston bore, independent of hydraulic circuit pressurization, thereby displacing the associated piston and maintaining clamping force through a self-locking or irreversible mechanical linkage, such as a ball-ramp assembly, screw-type mechanism, or wedge arrangement. A sealing arrangement disposed about the force transmission member maintains hydraulic integrity of the piston bore during both actuation modes, preventing fluid leakage while permitting relative axial sliding motion.

The disclosed caliper structure enables compact integration of redundant braking functions within a single housing, eliminating the need for a separate parking brake mechanism, drum, or cable-actuated auxiliary caliper, while maintaining full hydraulic service brake performance and reliable, fail-safe parking brake retention through mechanically self-sustaining force transmission.

# Brake Caliper Assembly Patent Summary

**Field:** This disclosure relates to a brake caliper assembly for use in vehicle braking systems, incorporating both service brake and park brake functionality.

**Summary:**

A brake caliper assembly (100) is disclosed comprising a caliper body having first and second caliper portions (104a, 104b) disposed on opposing sides of a rotor. The assembly includes first and second braking members (102a, 102b) positioned adjacent the caliper portions, configured to engage opposing friction surfaces of the rotor to generate braking force through frictional contact.

The caliper assembly further comprises first and second piston assemblies (108, 110) operably disposed within the respective caliper portions (104a, 104b). The piston assemblies are configured to translate axially in response to hydraulic or mechanical actuation, thereby urging the braking members (102a, 102b) into engagement with the rotor to effect service braking.

A park brake actuator (112) is integrated with the caliper assembly to provide a parking or emergency brake function independent of the primary hydraulic service brake system. The park brake actuator (112) is operably coupled to at least one of the piston assemblies (108, 110) via a force transmitting member (116), which is configured to convey an actuation force from the park brake actuator (112) to the associated piston assembly, causing displacement thereof sufficient to maintain the braking members (102a, 102b) in engagement with the rotor without continuous application of hydraulic pressure.

The force transmitting member (116) may comprise a mechanical linkage, cable, screw mechanism, or similar structure operable to convert an input actuation force (e.g., electric motor-driven, cable-actuated, or spring-based) into axial displacement of the piston assembly. This arrangement enables the brake caliper assembly (100) to selectively provide both dynamic service braking and static park/emergency braking functions within a unified, compact caliper structure, reducing component count and improving packaging efficiency relative to separate service and park brake mechanisms.

In operation, actuation of the piston assemblies (108, 110) via the standard hydraulic circuit provides service braking, while independent actuation of the park brake actuator (112) — transmitted through the force transmitting member (116) — engages the braking members (102a, 102b) for park brake application, holding the vehicle stationary without reliance on the hydraulic system.
